title: John Muir: Outdoor Enthusiast
summary: Josh and Chuck profile John Muir, the Scottish-American naturalist, writer and Sierra Club founder who was a driving force behind Yosemite becoming a national park. They cover his childhood in Wisconsin under a strict Calvinist father, his 1867 eye injury that turned him from inventing to studying nature, his thousand-mile walk to Florida and journey to California, his roughly six years in Yosemite as a sheep herder and writer, his marriage to Louisa Strentzel and her death in 1905, his friendship with Theodore Roosevelt, the Sierra Club's early campaigns, the Hetch Hetchy dam fight, and the racist views he held and how the national park system was built on forced evictions of Native Americans. The episode ends with a listener letter about cleft palate and a listener-mail segment about middle names.

entities.name: Ethnic Cleansing and America's Creation of National Parks

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to John Muir
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter, then introduce John Muir as synonymous with Yosemite and note his role in making it a national park and in wider preservation thinking.

segments.title: Muir's Scottish childhood and strict father
segments.summary: Muir was born in Dunbar, Scotland, and moved to Wisconsin at eleven. His stern Calvinist father was harsh, and the Wisconsin wilderness became Muir's refuge.

segments.title: Early inventions and the 1867 eye injury
segments.summary: Muir woke at 1 a.m. to have time for reading and tinkering, and built inventions including an early rising machine. He went to the Madison State Fair in 1860. In 1867 a tool pierced his eye, leaving him temporarily blind, and he gave up mechanical work to study nature.

segments.title: Walk to Florida and journey to California
segments.summary: After the injury Muir walked about a thousand miles to Cedar Key, Florida, caught malaria, sailed to Cuba and Panama, and reached San Francisco. He was then directed to Yosemite.

segments.title: Sheep herding and first years in Yosemite
segments.summary: Muir arrived in Yosemite in 1868 and stayed for about six years, working as a sheep herder and disliking sheep, which he called hoofed locusts. He documented the geology and botany, and wrote essays that made his name as a writer. Hosts describe Yosemite's mismanagement under state control, set by Lincoln's land grant.

segments.title: Marriage, farming, and Roosevelt camping trip
segments.summary: Muir married Louisa Strentzel in 1880 and farmed her family's fruit ranch in Martinez, California. Robert Underwood Johnson pushed him back to writing. Muir later camped with President Theodore Roosevelt in Yosemite, and they worked together on monuments such as Petrified Forest. Louisa died in 1905.

segments.title: Sierra Club and Muir's legacy and racism
segments.summary: Muir was the Sierra Club's first president and helped win the 1890 Yosemite and Mariposa Grove boundary expansion. The club later expanded nationally. The hosts discuss the Club's reckoning with Muir's racist views toward Native Americans and Black people, and how national parks were created through forced evictions, citing Isaac Cantor's 2007 article.

segments.title: Hetch Hetchy fight and Muir's death
segments.summary: Muir lost the fight to stop the damming of Hetch Hetchy Valley, which San Francisco wanted after the 1906 earthquake and fire. He died of pneumonia in 1914 at 76. The hosts note that no dam has been built on national park land since.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts sign off with the reading recommendation.
